headline: Where worldviews share ground and where they split
intro: Each sphere is an idea, drawn from the public writing and talks of the people on the map, on AI and society. Each diamond is a person. Select someone and the structure they stand on lights up.

Habermas called the background we reason from the lifeworld: it mostly goes unseen until something brings a piece of it into question. This map tries to do that on purpose, so that people can reason about the ground they stand on, and test whether they would sign how they are described.

schools.label: AI as a new kind of risk
schools.note: They see AI as a new kind of mind whose gravest dangers come from the systems themselves, not only from misuse, and they doubt that earlier technologies are a good guide.

schools.label: Human-first critics
schools.note: Market-driven technology doesn't serve people by itself, AI's promises are overblown, and rivalry with China is no reason to push ahead. The camp crosses left and right.

schools.label: Free-market builders
schools.note: AI won't concentrate power, the risk of extinction is overblown, and the state should stay out of directing AI.

schools.label: Skeptics of hype and of pausing
schools.note: AI's promises are overblown and it isn't a new kind of mind, but slowing it down would be wrong too; the dangers are in how people use it.

lenses.label: Accelerationism and AI safety
lenses.note: These camps were chosen by name, and the people in them sit in several measured schools.

findings.title: Accelerationism and AI safety share a picture of AI, and split on what to do
findings.body: Both sides hold that intelligence can run on silicon and that capable AI has no built-in reason to care for us. The split sharpens upward: at the action layer they oppose each other on 4 of 5 shared idea families. They also split at the roots, over whether collective choice can steer technology and whether intelligence can pair with any goal. E/acc does not form its own school here.

findings.title: The AI safety and AI ethics feud sits at the very bottom
findings.body: AI safety people and AI critics agree on all 6 shared families about knowing and all 8 about the world, and on 6 of 7 about action. They split on what language models are. If they could settle that one question, or set it aside, much of their conflict has less to stand on.

findings.title: Some alliances cross the usual lines
findings.body: Hawley sits with Bender, Gebru and Hao in 65% to 90% of reruns: Hawley and Bender share 18 ideas and oppose on none measured. Thiel and Karp share 5 ideas with no opposition yet rarely group together (7%), because most of what they write is about different things.

findings.title: Popular links can vanish, as Yarvin and Vance do
findings.body: They share one idea in what they argue and land in the same school in 2% of reruns. This sample can't rule out influence, and it shows no shared structure.

words: The same word can carry a different world. This compares the sentences each group builds around a word. A larger gap means the surroundings differ more. It catches a change of subject as well as a change of meaning, so read the examples before trusting a gap.
belonging: Habermas held that we cohere by giving reasons. Karp's dissertation argued that jargon binds groups by licensing aggression. These widely held ideas have the fewest argument links. That could mean they mostly mark membership, or that our link readers missed their reasons, so this is a lead to test.

p: We read public works by every person on the map: their own essays, talks and interviews. Each claim needs an exact quote, then passes code checks and a local entailment model. Positions on the 24 fingerprint statements were then re-read from the full texts by two blind readers, and only positions two independent readings support are shown.

Readers merged claims into shared ideas, each placed in a layer: being, knowing, values, world or action. Every holding then got a blind second reading, and we kept only what both readings agreed on. Saying nothing about an idea counts as missing, never as disagreement.

The layers draw on Apostel and Aerts's worldview components, Bourdieu's doxa and Habermas's lifeworld. Links use argument theory: Toulmin, Walton and ASPIC+. These are proposals, and the framing itself is open to dispute.

Thinkers rarely address the same exact claim. Only about a tenth of person and idea pairs have a recorded stance. So people are compared over 40 families of related ideas, with shared ground removed. Height is the layer and is fixed. Links pull supporting ideas together and push opposed ones apart, around measured positions.

Nobody placed here has seen this or agreed to it. All of it is provisional machine reading, and no person has ratified it. Each person is read from about three works, so dates mean first appearance in this sample and cannot show change over time. Twenty-seven hand-picked people show a pattern, not a population. School names are working labels, and the people named should replace them.

self: Worldviews have layers, and some assumptions sit deeper than others.
People's public words are fair evidence of what they hold.
Seeing a shared root can help people who disagree.
Describing a view in terms its holders would sign is a good, and agreement is not required.
Disagreement between camps deserves to be mapped, and the middle has no special standing.

c1.label: AI as a new kind of risk
c1.note: They see AI as a new kind of mind whose gravest dangers come from the systems themselves, not only from misuse, and they doubt that earlier technologies are a good guide.

c1.1.label: Slow it down and govern it
c1.1.note: They want the most powerful AI slowed and governed in public, would never let AI decide on its own to kill, doubt AI leaders are being honest about the risks, and reject racing China.

c1.1.1.label: Stop and regulate
c1.1.1.note: They hold all three together: the risk of extinction is real, frontier developers need binding rules, and the most powerful systems should be slowed or stopped.

c1.1.1.1.label: Kokotajlo and Bengio
c1.1.1.1.note: Loss of control and extinction come first for them, and authority over AI should stay with the public.

c1.1.2.label: Murphy and Harris
c1.1.2.note: The risk is real, the future is a choice, and productivity alone won't look after workers.

c1.2.label: Rationalists and long-termists
c1.2.note: They doubt collective choice can steer AI's course, think AI may come to deserve moral consideration, and want it slowed rather than raced against China.

c1.2.1.label: Yudkowsky, Musk and Alexander
c1.2.1.note: They trust their own reasoning over the average of expert opinion, take extinction risk seriously, and don't think strict rules now would do more harm than good.

c1.2.2.label: Hinton and MacAskill
c1.2.2.note: AI's promise is real and so is its risk: the danger to watch is the systems themselves, not only how people use them.

c1.3.label: Security realists
c1.3.note: Liberal ideals won't win on their own, the most capable models should stay closed, and the risk of extinction is real.

c1.4.label: Lab stewards
c1.4.note: AI is a new kind of mind, unlike any earlier technology, and where it takes society is still ours to choose.

c1.5.label: Hopeful builders
c1.5.note: They take the risk of extinction seriously and still see market-driven technology as good for people.

c1.6.label: Safety insiders
c1.6.note: Former and current lab insiders and critics: the risk is real, AI isn't hype, and the most capable models shouldn't be released openly.

c2.label: Human-first critics
c2.note: Market-driven technology doesn't serve people by itself, AI's promises are overblown, and rivalry with China is no reason to push ahead. The camp crosses left and right.

c2.1.label: Democratic humanists
c2.1.note: AI is a tool, not a mind, and how it reshapes work and society is a democratic choice.

c2.1.1.label: Power and labour critics
c2.1.1.note: On its current course AI concentrates wealth and power, the people it trains on should be paid, and the hype runs ahead of the facts.

c2.1.1.1.label: Merchant, Acemoglu, Weyl, Hawley and Hao
c2.1.1.1.note: Left and right together: the public, not executives or experts, should decide, and power is concentrating.

c2.2.label: Hype and harms critics
c2.2.note: Talk of extinction distracts from the harms AI does now; AI isn't a mind, and the hype is the problem.

c2.2.1.label: Whittaker and Gebru
c2.2.1.note: They reject the extinction framing and the idea of AI as a mind; its direction is a choice people make.

c3.label: Free-market builders
c3.note: AI won't concentrate power, the risk of extinction is overblown, and the state should stay out of directing AI.

c3.1.label: Human-centred builders
c3.1.note: AI is a tool that should serve people; work gives people dignity, and slowing AI down would be a mistake.

c3.1.1.label: Sacks and Andreessen
c3.1.1.note: Competition limits harm, fear of AI outruns the evidence, and extinction risk isn't real.

c3.1.2.label: Vance and Kratsios
c3.1.2.note: Technology's course is a choice for a free, self-governing people, and AI's promise is real.

c3.1.3.label: Zuckerberg and LeCun
c3.1.3.note: AI should serve people, misuse is the real danger, earlier technologies are a good guide, and models should be open.

c3.2.label: Accelerationists
c3.2.note: AI is a new kind of mind that may deserve moral consideration, and humanity needn't be its final end.

c3.2.1.label: Verdon and Cruz
c3.2.1.note: Fear outruns the evidence, markets serve people, and strict rules now would do more harm than good.

c3.2.2.label: Hanson and Rao
c3.2.2.note: Don't slow AI down: extinction risk isn't real, and humanity needn't be AI's final end.

c3.3.label: Progress optimists
c3.3.note: AI is a tool, markets serve people, and AI won't concentrate power in a few companies.

c4.label: Skeptics of hype and of pausing
c4.note: AI's promises are overblown and it isn't a new kind of mind, but slowing it down would be wrong too; the dangers are in how people use it.
